analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey places construction AI adoption at 14.9 percent of firms in the most recent period, up from 13.6 percent in the prior period. That fortnightly measure, drawn directly from firm responses, makes construction one of the more consistently tracked sectors in the federal dataset, even if adoption still sits well below a majority of businesses in the industry.

The Associated General Contractors of America, which represents over 27,000 member firms, surveys technology adoption and safety-technology compliance across US builders and serves as the primary trade-level adoption record for the sector. AGC has organized programming that brings together construction leaders, technology experts, and AI practitioners across two tracks of practical insights, a signal that interest has moved from curiosity to operational questions about implementation. BuiltWorlds, a global network focused on buildings and infrastructure professionals, tracks site robotics, jobsite IoT, and digital preconstruction across research programs and member benchmarking, and its annual AI and machine learning conference covers existing and emerging use cases across the full construction, building, and operations process, including case studies on specific solutions and lessons learned.

The use cases the sector is paying closest attention to include computer-vision safety monitoring, building information modeling clash detection, and autonomous site scanning. BuiltWorlds also examines AI infrastructure from a construction demand perspective, with its buildings conference placing specific emphasis on data centers and AI infrastructure as a growth area for the industry itself, meaning construction firms are simultaneously deploying AI and being hired to build the facilities that house it.

On the capital side, CREtech and MetaProp track venture flow across architecture, engineering, and construction technology alongside property technology more broadly. The JSON does not specify deal volumes or named funding rounds, so precise investment figures are not available from these sources, but the presence of dedicated proptech and contech trackers reflects enough capital activity to warrant ongoing monitoring.

For a decision-maker evaluating whether to deploy AI in construction, the Census data suggests roughly one in seven firms is already doing so and that share is growing, while AGC and BuiltWorlds both indicate the industry conversation has shifted toward practical implementation strategy and case-based learning rather than introductory awareness. The sources here do not report specific ROI figures or regulatory constraints, so those considerations would require additional research beyond what this material supports.
